claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A transformer model can be pretrained on synthetic materials data and fine-tuned on HEA data.
Phase-diagram-inspired descriptors can be integrated with machine learning to represent alloy phase stability.
Combining a transformer pretrained on synthetic HEA data with phase-diagram-derived microstructural descriptors is suitable for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The integrated model can predict Young's modulus for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The integrated model can predict yield strength for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The integrated model can predict toughness for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
Phase-diagram parameters capture the hierarchical alloy's multilevel chemical fluctuations and mediate their effects on mechanical properties.
Transformer self-attention captures intricate elemental interactions.
Transformer self-attention specifically captures long-range and nonlinear elemental interactions.
Phase-diagram-inspired descriptors provide physicochemical context for the model.
The synergy between self-attention and phase-diagram descriptors maps microstructural heterogeneity to macroscopic mechanical properties.
The integrated model will improve prediction accuracy for Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness by approximately 20–30% over the stated baseline.
The integrated model will reduce computational demand by about 50% relative to conventional CALPHAD and first-principles methods.
Maintaining the reported hierarchical structure during standardized tensile and fracture testing is required for validation.
The model will cease to be reliable if phase instability or inadequate training data and descriptors prevent accurate representation of critical microstructural features.
Non-equilibrium processing or severely altered chemical ordering may put the alloy outside the model's reliable domain.

A blinded prospective comparison will test predictions against standardized measurements and against conventional CALPHAD/first-principles predictions, with failure to meet the stated accuracy and computational thresholds defined as falsification.
